title: Self-invocation and a lock-free lazy proxy

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Inside OrderService, processOrders calls this.placeOrder(order) for each order, and placeOrder carries @Transactional. What happens to those calls?

options.text: Each call through this gets its own transaction from the Spring proxy.
options.says: The proxy only sees calls that come through it; this.placeOrder goes straight to the target object.

options.text: All calls through this share one transaction that the proxy opened.
options.says: processOrders is not @Transactional, so the proxy opens no transaction around it, and the inner calls never pass the proxy.

options.text: Calls through this reach the target directly, so no transaction starts.
options.says: The page's gotcha: self-invocation bypasses the proxy, so the @Transactional behaviour does not apply.

questions.stem: A virtual proxy creates its subject with ref.compareAndSet(null, new RealImageService(filename)). Two threads call display() first at the same moment. What can happen?

options.text: Both may build a service; compareAndSet keeps whichever lands earlier.
options.says: The page notes that racing threads may each construct an instance; compareAndSet then stores only the first.

options.text: One thread waits inside compareAndSet until the other has built its service.
options.says: compareAndSet takes no lock; that waiting describes the synchronized and double-checked versions.

options.text: Both may build a service, and compareAndSet lets each thread keep its own.
options.says: Each display() reads ref.get() after the compareAndSet, so every thread uses the one instance that was stored.

concepts: A lazy proxy built on AtomicReference.compareAndSet is lock-free but may create the real subject more than once, keeping only one.
A call a bean makes on itself through this bypasses its proxy, so the proxy's behaviour does not apply to it.
